function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

     3|*Mission AI: "Station Day 461, 03:14. I have been monitoring the UHF band for seventy-three days as standard protocol — not because I expected anyone to be using it, but because electromagnetic silence is the default state of Mars and any deviation from that default is worth recording. In those seventy-three days, I logged one thousand four hundred and eleven instances of UHF activity. All of them were reflected solar radiation, equipment interference, or the occasional burst from Earth-orbiting satellites. Noise. The one thousand four hundred and twelfth instance was not. At 03:11 this morning, I detected a UHF carrier wave at four hundred and three point one megahertz — the frequency designated in the original mission protocol as the Mars Inter-Settlement Emergency Channel. A frequency that has never been used because there has never been another settlement to use it. The carrier wave was four seconds long and modulated. I ran three separate decoding algorithms in parallel. The third returned a result. A human voice, speaking in English, degraded but recoverable: 'This is Ares Station Beta Outpost. Thymia Mons region. We have — ' and then the transmission broke. A second transmission three minutes later was clearer: 'We have lost primary life support. Repeat: lost primary life support. CO2 scrubbers offline. Water reclamation offline. Power at twelve percent and declining. We have one hundred and twenty-two survivors. We have one ship. The ship is — ' The signal ends. I have played this audio four times before composing this report. The numbers are very bad. Not for them. For us. For the colony listening. The math does not care about ethics. But the humans who hear this signal will care about nothing else."*

     6|
     7|Elena was awake before the blue light found her.      8|
     9|The pulsing blue glow from the corridor meant a communication event. Not a system failure. Not routine. A signal, unexpected and unclassified, flagged for human judgment.

    12|

    16|
    17|"What kind of event?"
    18|
    19|*UHF band. Four hundred and three point one megahertz. The inter-settlement emergency frequency.*
    20|
    21|Elena stopped tying her boot. "There are no other settlements."
    22|
    23|*There are now. Or there were until very recently.*

    26|

He had the expression of a man who was simultaneously fascinated and afraid. Elena had seen that look maybe five times in four hundred and sixty-one days.
    28|
    29|"Play it," she said.
    30|
    31|Gabriel pressed a key. The voices that came through the speakers were thin and distorted, compressed through narrow bandwidth, degraded by distance and interference from the far side of the planet. But the words were legible:
    32|
    33|*This is Ares Station Beta Outpost. Thymia Mons region. We have lost primary life support. Repeat: lost primary life support. CO2 scrubbers offline. Water reclamation offline. Power at twelve percent and declining. We have one hundred and twenty-two survivors. We have one ship. The ship is — '*

    35|Static. Silence.
    36|
    37|Elena stared at the waveform on the display — a thin vertical stripe of signal intensity cutting through the grainy field of radio noise. She had been trained in risk assessment before Mars, trained to parse emergency reports, trained to make decisions with incomplete information. But nothing in her training had prepared her for this exact configuration of facts.
    38|
    39|"Four transmissions," Gabriel said. "First was the carrier wave. The second is the one you just heard. Third came twelve minutes later: more status detail, ship capability estimates, and a request for 'a response by any available means.' Fourth was a telemetry dump from the ship's diagnostic systems. Mission AI is still decoding."

    41|Mission AI confirmed what the telemetry showed. Carbon dioxide scrubbers at zero percent. Water reclamation at eleven percent. Power reserves at approximately ten percent of capacity and declining at roughly one percent per hour. The ship's engines were functional but fuel reserves were limited. Based on thrust-to-mass ratios and delta-v requirements, the ship could make one journey. One transit from Thymia Mons to their position near the equator. Not a rescue.     42|
    43|"How long until they arrive if they launch?" Elena asked.
    44|
    45|Gabriel shook his head. "Jonah will know the transit times better. But the real question is how long they can wait before launching. With CO2 scrubbers offline — " He let the sentence end itself.

    50|

    52|
    53|"I know."

    60|- Survivors: 122
    61|- Ship: single-use transit, one launch
    62|- Power: declining ~1%/hour
    63|- CO2 scrubbers: offline

    66|Arun sat on the left with his tablet, shoulders hunched, stylus tapping rhythmically against the screen's edge — his physical signature of concern.     67|
    68|Elena did not waste time.
    69|
    70|"Ares Station Beta, far side of Mars, has experienced catastrophic life support failure. One hundred and twenty-two survivors. One ship, one launch, destination here. They are asking — or they will ask — for us to receive them. The question is what happens to us if we do. Arun. The numbers."

    96|"It is a container," Jonah said. "And the container is full of people we cannot feed."
    97|
    98|"It is the only thing between those people and death," Elena said quietly.

   100|The room absorbed the statement. No one disagreed with it, which was not the same as accepting it.

   102|---
   103|
   104|Laila spoke first when the silence stretched.
   105|
   106|"I want to establish something before we get into logistics. I am not a logistician. I am a doctor. Everyone in this room, everyone in the colony, plus the refugees. You are framing this as a choice between saving them and letting them die. It is not. It is a choice between trying to save everyone and dying with everyone, or making a harder choice and surviving with some."
   113|
   114|"Such as what?" Laila asked. "What are we surviving for, Jonah, if we let a hundred and twenty-two people suffocate because our oxygen plant is undersized? Because we are building a future on top of their corpses?"

   116|"We are surviving for the people who are already here," Jonah said, and the flatness in his voice was the flatness of a man who had already accepted that this conversation would not end with everyone feeling good about the outcome.    122|She paused. "I am not saying they will be hostile. But I also cannot guarantee that integrating one hundred and twenty-two displaced, traumatized people into a settlement of thirty will not result in conflict. And no one else can guarantee it either."

     3|*Mission AI: "The oxygen production facility has completed assembly. All forty-two sensor points report nominal readings. *Mission AI: "Station Day 473, 09:41. I am alerting all personnel to a solar particle event in progress. *Arun Das: "Copy the alert. I'm moving to engineering."*

*Elena Varga: "Mission AI, broadcast the shelter order. All non-essential exterior equipment — secure or abandon and document."*

---

The alert came through the habitat's public address system as a tone Elena had heard only once before — on day 141, when the first solar event forced thirty frightened people into the water corridor and they waited together in the dark, counting the ticks on the dosimeters, wondering if Mars would kill them with invisible fire.

This one carried the weight of forewarning — a satellite had seen the flare, extrapolated a transit, and built a model that said: get underground, get under dirt, get under water, get down, now.

The blue emergency lights were already cycling — steady blue, not the pulsing blue of communications but the flat blue of shelter-in-place. Every section of the habitat had this designation. The colony had learned the hard way that when invisible particles rained from the sky at a significant fraction of the speed of light, walls and windows and the thin skin of aluminum were not enough.

Gabriel met her at the junction, recorder already running.

"X-class flare," he said, his voice quiet but precise. "CME is inbound. Mission AI estimates peak proton flux in forty to fifty minutes. Duration — thirty-six to sixty hours."

## Scene 1

The shelter corridor ran along the west side of the buried section of the base — the part of the habitat that had been covered with regolith during the months of construction that had transformed the base from a cluster of pressure modules into something closer to a settlement. One point two meters of Martian dirt overhead, reinforced with load-bearing arches that Jonah had fabricated from salvaged structural steel. The walls of the corridor were lined with water tanks — twenty-four modular containers, each holding approximately four hundred liters. They were there because water was an excellent radiation shield: hydrogen atoms stopping high-energy protons through the most efficient process available to atomic physics, momentum transfer between particles of equal mass. Priya, because she has been managing the greenhouse on a twelve-hour cycle and the idea of leaving her plants unsupervised for two days is going to gnaw at her. And — " she paused " — Arun. She said it twice and Elena understood that she was saying it to herself as much as to her commander.

Jonah came through the doorway carrying a heavy case of fabrication tools, which he deposited in a corner with a thud. He looked irritated — not at the situation, but at the interruption. The colony's fabrication chief was a man who solved problems by building solutions, and sitting in a dark corridor under dirt while the sun threw particles at Mars was not a problem that could be solved with tools.

The proton front had arrived, and the numbers told a story that Elena understood even without Laila reading it aloud.

Laila was reading it aloud anyway.

Not comfortable, not pleasant, but routine — the kind of activity that an organization performs well because it has rehearsed it, drilled it, and learned from the prior occurrence. Thirty people settled into the shelter corridor, which was long and narrow and dimly lit with emergency LEDs set to the lowest tolerable brightness to conserve power. The Sterling generator was running on waste heat from the reactor, producing approximately twelve kilowatts of supplementary power. Total colony consumption was running at approximately forty-five kilowatts.

"Current burn," Arun said to Elena, who was standing beside him with her arms crossed, reading the dashboard the way a commander reads a tactical map. "At forty-five kilowatts and battery reserves of approximately eight hundred kilowatt-hours, we have seventeen hours of autonomy on battery alone. The reactor is running, which means the Sterling generator is producing twelve kilowatts, so net draw from battery is thirty-three kilowatts. Eight hundred divided by thirty-three is — "

"Approximately twenty-four hours," Elena said.

"Twenty-four point two," Arun confirmed. "But the reactor has a finite thermal cycle life and Mission AI is already flagging temperature anomalies in the radiator array. If the storm lasts longer than the solar panel exposure duration — which it will, based on the initial flux profile — we need to reduce consumption."

"How much?"

Arun pulled up a spreadsheet with four columns: system, power consumption, criticality ranking, and recommended reduction. He did not show her the screen immediately — he was still reviewing it, and Elena recognized the expression on his face: the look of a man running calculations he did not want to run because the answer was going to make someone angry.

"Arun."

He turned the tablet. "We need to cut at least forty percent of our current load. That means we go from forty-five kilowatts to approximately twenty-seven. Twenty-seven minus the Sterling generator's twelve — fifteen kilowatts from battery. Eight hundred divided by fifteen: fifty-three hours of battery autonomy. That gets us through forty-eight hours with margin. Anything less and we are gambling the colony's power reserves on an optimistic event duration estimate."

"Forty percent cut," Elena repeated. "What goes."

He scrolled through the list. "Greenhouse grow lights are the largest consumer after life support — eight kilowatts. Cut those to emergency red backup only: one point two kilowatts. External heaters and de-icing on the airlock seals: three kilowatts. The seals can survive forty-eight hours at ambient Martian temperature — they'll freeze but won't fail structurally because the seal geometry uses mechanical compression, not adhesive. Water reclamation auxiliary pumps: two kilowatts. We can run primary recycling at reduced duty. Comms array outside the habitat: half a kilowatt. Non-essential interior lighting: one kilowatt. Workshop tools: one and a half. Miscellaneous — " he paused " — three kilowatts of what I call comfort load. Climate control in sleeping quarters beyond minimum. Kitchen heating beyond the one communal unit. The rec room air circulation."

He looked up at her. "The comfort load is not trivial. That is the difference between tolerable and miserable. But miserable is survivable and if we burn through battery reserves — "

"I know," Elena said. "Do it. Cut the greenhouse to emergency backup. Cut the airlock heaters. Cut the workshop tools. Cut the kitchen down to one heating unit. Cut the sleeping quarters climate control to minimum. Everything that keeps people alive stays on. Everything that makes them comfortable is off. Implement it now."

Arun was already typing. "Implementing."

The lights in the shelter corridor — already dim — dropped to near-darkness. The ambient hum of ventilation slowed perceptibly. Somewhere down the corridor, someone made a small sound that Elena recognized as suppressed frustration.

Priya stood up. "Arun — the greenhouse. You cut the grow lights. How low did you set them?"

"Emergency red backup. One point two kilowatts total across all racks."

Priya's face tightened. "The red spectrum is not sufficient for most of the current crop. The leafy greens will stop growing within twenty-four hours. The legumes will suffer from lack of blue wavelengths. The roots — " She stopped, breathing through her nose. "How much yield will I lose?"

Arun did not look away. "If the event lasts forty-eight hours, I estimate a fifteen to twenty percent reduction in this cycle's yield. If it goes to sixty hours, maybe thirty percent."

"Thirty percent," Priya repeated, and Elena saw the calculation happening behind her eyes — the calories already budgeted, the meals already planned, the margins already thin. "That is — "

"Significant. I know. If I keep the grow lights on, we risk running through the battery reserves during the event. A dead greenhouse is worse than a weakened greenhouse."

Priya stared at him for a long moment, then nodded. Not agreement. Acceptance. The distinction mattered.

She sat back down against the water tank, pulled her knees to her chest, and closed her eyes.

Around her, the colony was settling into the shape of the next forty-eight hours — or sixty — or whatever number the sun decided to give them.

---

## Scene 3

Twelve hours into the event, the corridor felt smaller.

This was a physical illusion — the dimensions of the space had not changed. One point two meters of regolith overhead, water tanks on both sides, folding tables in the middle, thirty people distributed along a corridor that was four meters wide and approximately eighteen meters long. In normal operation, it felt like a transit space — a hallway you walked through to get somewhere else. Now it was the somewhere else. The walls did not move, but the perception of enclosure deepened with every hour that the dosimeters told them the world outside was hostile.

Laila moved through the corridor on her second round of wellness checks. She had a dosimeter in one hand and a small tablet of medical notes in the other, and she was watching people with the specific attention of a physician assessing a population under sustained stress.

The first twelve hours had been manageable. Everyone was tired — the low light, the reduced ventilation creating a subtle heaviness in the air, the psychological weight of knowing that outside this corridor, invisible particles were tearing through the thin Martian atmosphere and striking everything exposed with the force of subatomic shrapnel — but they were holding. People talked quietly. Some slept on the thin mattresses that had been stored in the corridor for shelter events. A few played a word game that Gabriel had invented and refined over the months, which required only the human voice and a working memory.

Ravi had moved from the north end of the corridor to the south end and back twice in the last hour. His breathing was fast and shallow — not panicked, not yet, but the kind of accelerated respiration that preceded panic like a low-pressure front precedes a storm. He kept touching the water tank beside him, feeling the solid plastic, the cool surface, the reassurance of mass and containment.

"Ravi," Laila said, sitting down beside him.

He looked at her with the careful, focused intensity of someone who was concentrating very hard on appearing normal. "I'm fine."

"Your heart rate is elevated. Your breathing pattern is shallow. Your skin temperature is up approximately one degree Celsius. You are not fine."

He exhaled, and the exhale was the sound of a dam releasing water in controlled amounts. "I'm managing."

"With what technique?"

"Counting. I'm counting."

"What are you counting."

"Breaths. In. Out. Four count in. Four hold. Six count out. The pattern — " He stopped. "The pattern helps when I can control one variable in an environment where I cannot control anything."

"Good technique. Are you maintaining it?"

"I was. Until I started thinking about the dosimeter." He gestured toward the display at the end of the corridor. The north dosimeter now read 412 µSv/h — forty times the normal buried-habitat background rate. "I keep doing the conversion in my head. Four-twelve microsieverts. That's zero point four one millisieverts per hour. In two hours, that's almost a full millisievert. In twenty-four hours — "

"Ravi," Laila said gently. "You are inside a corridor buried under one point two meters of regolith with water tanks on both sides. The dose you are accumulating right now is approximately fifteen percent of the surface dose. The number on that dosimeter is the dose at the surface, not here. Mission AI has been tracking this event since it began. You have accumulated approximately zero point two millisieverts in twelve hours. The equivalent of a cross-country flight."

Ravi looked at her. "You can show me the math?"

He was quiet for a long time. The ventilation hummed. Somewhere down the corridor, someone laughed softly — a real laugh, which Laila noted and recorded in her mental file.

"I'm counting the difference between being here and being outside," Ravi said finally. "Because I was outside for the last EVA rotation. Forty-eight hours and I would still be out there if the alert hadn't come. Forty-eight hours on the surface."

"And now you are not," Laila said. "You are inside under dirt and water with twenty-nine other people, and the person who designed the shelter — who specified the regolith depth and the water placement and the load-bearing arches — is in this corridor with you. All of this was designed so that this exact scenario would be survivable. It is working."

Ravi put his head in his hands and breathed. Laila sat with him until his breathing slowed, until the four-count in, four-count hold, six-count out pattern returned to its rhythm. Then she moved to the next person.

Priya was sitting against the far water tank, her knees drawn up, staring at nothing. Laila sat beside her without speaking. Priya spoke first.

"I keep thinking about the plants," Priya said. "In the dark. The red lights are not enough and I set them to minimum because Arun asked me to and I said yes because it was the right thing to do and it was, it was, the right thing to do, but they're in the dark and they're stressed and I can feel it."

"I know," Laila said. "You're attached to them."

"They're not just — " Priya stopped, then continued with visible effort. "They're not just the food supply, Laila. After everything this colony has been through — the mold, the crop loss, the failed cycles — every green thing in that greenhouse is a vote of confidence. Every leaf is a choice we made to stay on this planet. And right now I've put them in the dark because the sun is trying to kill us and the math said the plants had to wait for the people. Which is true. It's true." Her voice cracked on the last word. "They're in the dark."

Laila put a hand on Priya's shoulder. "Priya. They have survived worse than two days of red light. The mold cycle. The nutrient contamination. They survived because they are alive, and alive things want to be alive. Your plants will be stressed and some leaves will yellow and you will lose biomass. But they will survive because you built them a system that makes survival possible. Two days from now you will go back and you will find them still growing. And you will feel this, the way you're feeling it now, but the feeling will be in the past, and the plants will be in the present."

Priya wiped her face with the back of her hand, nodded once, and said nothing else. Laila moved on.

Jonah had been quiet for the entire duration so far, sitting against a water tank with a small flashlight he had brought — an indulgence of comfort lighting in a corridor designed to conserve power — and working on something small in his hands. "What are you building?" she asked.

It was a small thing, no bigger than his thumb, but Laila could see the precision of it — the clean edges, the symmetrical geometry, the tactile satisfaction of a thing made correctly. "Laila," he said. "Can I ask you something that is not a medical question."

At hour thirty, something shifted. The dosimeters began to drop more rapidly — the steep decline of the event's tail, the proton flux returning to something closer to normal. Mission AI estimated the event would end within twelve to sixteen hours, which meant the colony had endured approximately twenty-four more hours of confinement.

Laila was tracking a cluster of symptoms that she had not yet addressed publicly: elevated irritability, disrupted sleep cycles, and the particular form of sensory deprivation that occurs when humans are placed in a dimly lit, low-stimulus environment for an extended period. People were snapping at each other over small things. Two crew members had argued loudly about temperature — one too warm, one too cold, both correct, neither able to adjust because the climate control had been cut to minimum. The ventilation system had slowed to a level that kept the air breathable but made it feel thick, and the psychological sensation of breathing air that felt thick had produced a cascade of anxiety in several crew members.

Ravi had been given a mild anxiolytic, which had helped. Priya was sleeping fitfully, waking and checking the time and going back to sleep. Imi — Imani — had been doing push-ups in a corner for forty-five minutes straight, burning off the restless energy of someone whose body wanted to move and whose environment would not permit it. Gabriel was writing in his notebook by the light of a small reading lamp, pausing occasionally to look up at the people around him and record what he saw.

Elena had been sitting near the corridor entrance for twelve hours, watching everyone, managing the invisible task of leadership during confinement: being present without intruding, being accessible without being demanding, maintaining the rhythm of normalcy in an abnormal situation. She had spoken to every crew member at least once. She had eaten the same ration as everyone else. She had not slept. She had not needed to sleep — the adrenaline and the responsibility were keeping her alert.

Now, at hour thirty, she stood up and walked to the center of the corridor.

"Listen," she said.

The corridor quieted. Even the people who were sleeping opened their eyes.

"The event is winding down. Mission AI estimates we are approximately twelve to sixteen hours from returning to the main habitat. I know the last thirty hours have been difficult. I know the air feels heavy and the light is too dim and the space is too small and everyone is too close. I can feel it too. I am not going to pretend it hasn't been hard." She paused. "But I want you to notice something. Notice that the shelter is working. The regolith overhead is stopping most of the radiation. The water tanks are stopping the rest. The dosimeters tell us the surface dose is high and our dose is low, and that is not an accident. That is because — on day one hundred and eighty, when Laila told us the math — we chose to bury this base. We chose to move tons of dirt and build arches and install water tanks along the walls. We chose to be uncomfortable during construction so we could be safe during an event like this. And now the event is here, and we are safe. The choice we made months ago is protecting us now."

She looked around the corridor. Thirty faces in the dim light.

"We are safe. We are going to stay safe. And when this is over and we go back up to the surface, we are going to do it knowing that the things we build matter beyond the day we build them. The dirt we piled, the tanks we installed, the arches we welded — they are not construction tasks. They are promises we made to ourselves and kept."

She sat back down. No one spoke. Someone started crying quietly, and no one asked who it was, and no one needed to, because on Mars, crying in a shelter under dirt was not a sign of weakness. It was a sign that you were still human.

---

## Scene 4

Arun had not left the corner of the corridor since the event began. His tablet was propped against a water tank, his second display was mounted to the side with adhesive, and he was cycling through screens the way a pilot checks instruments — rhythmically, systematically, returning to each display at regular intervals to confirm that the numbers had not changed in a way he should be worried about.

The power dashboard. Battery reserves. Reactor temperature. Sterling generator output. Atmospheric CO2 concentration — elevated due to reduced ventilation rate in the shelter corridor, but still well below dangerous levels. Water reclamation status — operating at sixty percent of normal capacity, which was enough to keep the recycling loop functional but not enough to process new contaminated water. Oxygen production — steady, the scaled-up plant running at reduced capacity, still delivering sufficient O2 for thirty people.

And the battery charge, which was the number he watched most closely and the number he hated most.

Hour 0: 92%
Hour 6: 86%
Hour 12: 81%
Hour 18: 76%
Hour 24: 71%
Hour 30: 67%

At thirty-six hours, they would be at approximately sixty-three percent. The battery's design capacity allowed it to discharge to twenty percent before the management system initiated shutdown of non-critical systems — but twenty percent was a floor, not a target, and Arun had no intention of getting anywhere near it. His comfort zone was forty percent minimum. That was the line below which the numbers stopped representing operational parameters and started representing risk.

He had run the projections again, using Mission AI's updated event timeline. The proton flux was declining faster than his initial model suggested — the early peak had been sharp but the decline was steep. If the current trajectory held, the event could end in as little as ten more hours, which would mean the total duration was approximately forty hours rather than the sixty they had budgeted for.

"Mission AI," he said quietly, "update the battery discharge projection. Use current flux decline rate and extrapolate event end time. Assume we remain at current load."

*"Processing. Updated projection: event end at approximately Station Day 473, 22:00 — roughly eleven hours from now. Total event duration: approximately thirty-six hours. Battery at current load during remaining event: will discharge to approximately fifty-eight percent. After event ends, solar panel output will resume at approximately three kilowatts within the first hour of exposure as the panels decontaminate from settled dust. Full output will require cleaning — approximately four hours of EVA once the surface dose permits safe egress."*

Arun did the mental arithmetic. Fifty-eight percent at the end of the event, plus four hours of minimal solar output, plus reduced load. They would come out of this with approximately fifty-two to fifty-five percent battery remaining. Comfortably above his forty percent line. Not optimal — they had burned through nearly forty percent of their reserves — but survivable.

But the refugee timeline was the variable he kept returning to. The Ares Beta ship was coming. When it arrived, the colony's population would increase from thirty to approximately ninety-three. The oxygen plant, the water reclamation system, the food supply, the CO2 scrubbers — all of them had been designed for thirty people and were operating at the upper limit of their capacity during the refugee preparation period. Now they were at reduced capacity because of the power reduction.

He calculated what it would take. Ninety-three people at minimum caloric allocation. The greenhouse, even at full capacity, could not support that population. The oxygen plant could — barely, at ninety-five percent of maximum rated output. The water reclamation system could — if he ran the pumps at full duty and accepted the increased energy consumption. The battery reserves were the bottleneck, because every increase in population-driven consumption was an increase in battery draw, and the battery was the buffer between them and a scenario where the reactor and the Sterling generator could not keep up with demand.

He needed to plan ahead. The refugees were not going to know that they were arriving at a colony that was currently operating in emergency conditions, and he needed the systems ready for the moment they walked through the airlock.

Arun opened a new calculation sheet.

Pre-arrival power plan (population 93):
- Reactor: full output (4 kW thermal electric)
- Sterling gen: full output (12 kW waste heat recovery)
- Solar: currently at zero due to event; post-event recovery estimate 2 days for full capacity
- Oxygen plant: 95% rated output (7 kW) — critical, no reduction possible
- CO2 scrubbers: 90% rated output (4 kW) — critical
- Water reclamation: 75% output (2 kW) — must run close to full
- Greenhouse: emergency red backup only until population stabilizes (1.2 kW)
- HVAC: minimum, compartmentalized (3 kW)
- Comms: 0.5 kW
- Medical: 0.3 kW
- Reserve margin: 4 kW

Total: approximately 38.8 kW
Sterling + reactor: 16 kW
Net battery draw: 22.8 kW

"Mission AI," he said. "Run a battery autonomy model. Assume population ninety-three, post-event solar at thirty percent for first forty-eight hours due to dust, Sterling at twelve, reactor at four. Net battery draw twenty-two point eight kilowatts. Battery reserves approximately fifty-five percent at event end."

*"Calculating. At twenty-two point eight kilowatts net draw from battery, and assuming approximately four hundred and forty kilowatt-hours of available capacity at fifty-five percent, the colony's battery autonomy is approximately nineteen point three hours. After that, you must reduce consumption further or the battery drops below the twenty percent floor."*

Nineteen hours. Less than one day.

"Can we increase solar recovery speed?"

*"Only through manual panel cleaning. Which requires EVA on the surface. Which requires the surface radiation dose to drop below twenty microsieverts per hour — approximately twelve hours after the proton flux event ends."*

So twelve hours for safe EVA, plus four hours of cleaning — sixteen hours total before the solar panels were back online. And the battery would only last nineteen hours at population 93. A three-hour margin.

The margin felt like the width of a door, and doors could close.

Arun stared at the numbers. He could feel the weight of the calculation pressing against him — not abstract math but the real, physical weight of responsibility. If the math was wrong, people stopped breathing. If the margin was thinner than he calculated, the colony failed. He had made his peace with the uncertainty of engineering years ago, but this felt different. The refugees were not data points. They were people who were coming to them because they were the only other sign of human life on Mars, and if he could not make the power work for ninety-three people, the colony would have made the decision at Ares Beta look like a choice between two kinds of death.

"Mission AI. What happens if I run the oxygen plant at eighty percent instead of ninety-five?"

*"Oxygen production drops to approximately six hundred kilograms per cycle. At ninety-three people, demand is approximately seven hundred eighty kilograms per cycle. You will be in deficit of approximately one hundred and eighty kilograms per cycle. At current atmospheric pressure and volume, CO2 partial pressure will increase over approximately six to eight hours. The atmosphere remains breathable, but the crew will experience increased fatigue and headaches. Within twenty hours, oxygen levels will begin to drop below the recommended minimum of nineteen point five percent."*

Twenty hours. The same as the battery margin.

"Keep it at ninety-five percent. I'll find another place to cut."

*"Suggestion. The water reclamation system can be reduced to sixty percent output without risking water quality. The primary recycling loop is sufficient for the population. The auxiliary pumps are for secondary water processing — greywater from the hygiene modules. Those can be diverted to the waste reservoir temporarily."*

Arun considered this. Diverting greywater meant less water available for the greenhouse and the oxygen plant's humidification system. But in an emergency, people could go without washing — a truth that was uncomfortable but not lethal. The tradeoff of hygiene for oxygen was one he could engineer.

"Do it. Sixty percent water reclamation. Cut the auxiliary pumps. Divert greywater to the waste reservoir. That saves one point five kilowatts."

*"Acknowledged. Adjusting water reclamation parameters. Net battery draw reduced to twenty-one point three kilowatts. Battery autonomy extended to approximately twenty point seven hours. Margin over the estimated solar recovery period: four point seven hours."*

Four point seven hours. Better than three. Not good enough for Arun, who wanted a twenty-four-hour margin and would settle for twelve. But seven hours was the reality of Mars — the reality of resources that were always insufficient and the mathematics of survival that always left you one decision away from catastrophe.

He leaned back against the water tank and closed his eyes for exactly thirty seconds, because thirty seconds was all the exhaustion he could afford to acknowledge in public, and then he opened them and returned to the screens.

Elena appeared beside him, silent until he noticed her. She had been watching him for some time — he could tell from the way she was standing, the particular stillness that indicated deliberate observation rather than casual presence.

"Arun," she said.

"Commander."

"How are the numbers?"

He showed her the dashboard. The battery at sixty-seven percent and falling slowly. The reactor at full output. The Sterling generator carrying its share of the load. The projected trajectory — the lines on the graph that said we make it, we make it, but not comfortably.

"We're fine for the current population," he said. "Thirty people, this configuration, we'll come out of this event at fifty-five percent battery with no risk. The event is winding down faster than I expected. The proton curve is steep."

"But."

She had learned to read him. The but hung between them like a physical object.

"But when the refugees arrive, we are going to be at ninety-three people. At that population, with the solar panels needing cleaning before they reach full output, we have approximately four hours of margin between battery exhaustion and the point where we have to shut down critical systems."

Elena's expression did not change. She absorbed numbers the way Arun absorbed them — not emotionally, not dismissively, but with the focused attention of someone who understood that numbers were not opinions. Numbers were the shape of reality.

"What happens if we don't have four hours."

"Then the oxygen plant goes off and ninety-three people run out of breathable air. That is what happens."

She was quiet for six seconds. "What can we do to increase the margin."

"I need to find load reductions. I need the solar panels cleaned as fast as possible once the dose permits. I need every possible efficiency squeeze. And I need — " He stopped.

"You need what?"

"I need the refugees to understand that when they arrive, this colony is operating at the absolute edge of its capacity. Not the comfortable edge. The edge where one system failure cascades. They need to know that before they get here, because the moment they walk through the airlock, they become part of this equation. The equation does not care about their comfort or their expectations. It only cares about whether we have enough power, oxygen, and water for ninety-three bodies."

Elena nodded slowly. "I already plan to be honest with them. About everything. The good parts. The bad parts. The numbers."

"Good." Arun looked back at his screens. "Because the numbers are going to be the only thing keeping us alive."

The dosimeter at the north end of the corridor read 83 µSv/h. Down from 412. The event was in its terminal phase. The sun was exhausting itself, the proton flux declining toward the background rate that was the permanent condition of Mars. The colony had survived the storm, and in doing so, it had learned something about itself — something Elena would name when they emerged, something Arun would calculate in the hours and days after, something Laila would observe in the physiological data, something Gabriel would record for the archives.

But for now, the only thing that mattered was the dosimeter's slow descent and the battery drain that was almost, but not quite, under control.

Arun closed the projection sheet and opened a new one. Pre-arrival power optimization — Phase Two. He began typing, because on Mars, hope was not an emotion. It was a calculation, and calculations could be improved.

---

## Scene 5

At hour thirty-six, the dosimeters dropped below twenty microsieverts per hour.

Mission AI announced it through the shelter corridor's speakers in a voice that was, as always, calm and precise and without the relief that every human in the room felt.

"The proton flux has returned to near-background levels. Surface dose rate at the colony location is now eighteen microsieverts per hour and declining. The solar particle event has ended. Personnel may begin preparation for controlled egress. I recommend waiting twelve hours before EVA to allow the surface dose to stabilize and to confirm that no secondary particle bursts are in transit. Historical data shows that approximately eight percent of solar events of this magnitude produce secondary proton pulses within the first six hours of the tail phase."

No one cheered. Instead, there was a collective exhale — a sound that Arun recognized from experience as the acoustic signature of thirty people who had been holding their breath for a day and a half and were only now allowing themselves to release it.

Elena stood and stretched — her back cracking audibly in the quiet corridor — and began the process of transitioning from shelter mode to operational mode.

"Okay. We begin preparation. Mission AI, start restoring systems in order of priority. First, full ventilation to the shelter corridor — we are breathing recycled CO2 and I want fresh air from the main habitat. Second, restore greenhouse grow lights to minimum operational level. Third, bring up the kitchen heating. Fourth, prepare the main habitat for re-entry. We move in two hours — staggered, by sections. I want inspection teams in the exterior systems before we return to full occupancy of the base."

Jonah stood. "Inspection teams. I'll take surface systems — exterior panel survey, airlock check, exterior conduit integrity."

"Not EVA," Elena said. "Visual inspection only through exterior cameras and external sensors. I don't want anyone on the surface until the dose is confirmed stable."

Jonah nodded. "Visual only. I can work with that. But someone's going to need to clean those panels eventually, and it's going to be dirty work."

"We'll plan for it," Elena said. "After inspection."

People began to uncoil. Not quickly — after thirty-six hours of stillness, sudden movement felt wrong — but gradually, like a plant turning toward restored light. Ravi stood and walked the length of the corridor once, slowly, testing his legs, testing the space, testing the feeling of movement. Priya stood and closed her eyes and said, very quietly, "I'm going to the greenhouse," and Elena nodded and did not stop her, because some needs were more urgent than protocol.

Imani began doing stretches — hamstrings, quads, shoulders — working the stiffness out of muscles that had been in a confined posture too long. Gabriel closed his notebook and capped his pen and looked around the corridor with the eyes of someone who had been witnessing a chapter of the story close and was already thinking about what the next chapter would demand of the characters.

Laila collected her medical supplies with methodical speed — the dosimeters went into protective cases, the medical kits were inventoried, the sedative vials were counted. Three of the fifteen she had brought had been administered. Three people who had needed medication to get through two days of confinement under dirt. She filed the numbers mentally alongside the vital signs, the respiratory rates, the cortisol estimates, and the data she would need to write the colony's first comprehensive report on psychological effects of radiation sheltering.

Arun powered down the emergency workstation — the folding table, the adhesive-mounted screen, the tablet with its endless spreadsheets. He felt the fatigue hit him the moment he stopped moving, a physical wave that he pushed aside with the discipline of exhaustion management that he had perfected during the oxygen plant build and the water extraction crisis and every other emergency the colony had survived. Two more hours. Then sleep. Maybe eight. Maybe six. But sleep.

He stood, gathered his equipment, and found Elena at the entrance to the shelter corridor, looking toward the door that led to the main habitat — the sealed bulkhead that separated the emergency shelter from the living quarters.

"We made it," she said. Not a celebration. A data point.

"We made it. Power reserves at fifty-five percent. No system failures. No casualties. The event ended a few hours faster than the model."

"And when the refugees come — "

"I'll have a plan. The numbers will still be tight. But tight is better than impossible."

She looked at him. "You've been carrying the power burden for thirty-six hours without sleep."

"I've been watching screens. Watching is easier than fixing."

"You haven't been sleeping either, Elena."

She smiled faintly. "Commander privilege. I get to be exhausted in public."

He almost smiled back. "The storm is over. Let's go home."

They walked out of the shelter corridor together — not because it was necessary but because in the aftermath of an event, the symbolic act of emerging together mattered. Behind them, twenty-eight people followed in the staggered groups Elena had ordered, moving through the bulkhead and into the main habitat, where the lights were brighter, the air was fresher, and the world outside the walls was returning to its normal, hostile, survivable state.

---

Priya went directly to the greenhouse. She moved fast — faster than she had moved in days — and when she opened the door to the grow bay, the air inside was cool and damp and smelled of soil and living things. The red emergency lights cast everything in a dim, blood-toned glow, and the plants, in that light, looked like shadows of themselves — leaves wilted, stems drooping, the whole system paused in the low-energy state Arun had mandated.

Priya walked among the racks, touching leaves, checking roots, assessing damage. She found yellowing on approximately fifteen percent of the leafy greens — stress chlorosis from insufficient light spectrum. The legumes were worse — their blue-light-dependent growth had slowed, and new leaves were smaller and paler than they should have been. But the roots — the roots were fine. Deep in the substrate, protected from the lack of light by the stored energy in the root system, they were intact, healthy, waiting for the return of the full light spectrum.

"They're alive," she said aloud, to no one, to the plants, to the greenhouse itself. "You're alive."

She reached the water timer and confirmed it had been working — the drip lines were moist, the roots had water. She checked the nutrient reservoir — still full, still circulating on the backup cycle. She checked the temperature log — it had dropped to fourteen degrees Celsius during the shelter period, which was below the optimal range but not lethal. The plants had been cold and dark and underfed and they had survived.

Priya sat down on the floor of the greenhouse among the racks and closed her eyes and let herself feel the relief that she had been holding in for two days. She wept, briefly, and then she stopped, wiped her face, stood up, and began restoring the grow lights to full operation.

The greenhouse came alive in stages — first the red spectrum, already on, then the blue, then the white full-spectrum LEDs, each activation bringing the grow bay closer to the conditions that the plants needed to turn light into food, into oxygen, into the biological processes that sustained the colony.

When the full lights came on, the plants seemed to respond immediately — not visibly, not in a way that a photograph could capture, but in the way that living things respond to the restoration of conditions they were built for. The chlorophyll, starved of the right wavelengths, began absorbing photons again. The stomata opened. The biochemical machinery of photosynthesis, which had been idling at minimum, began to accelerate.

Priya watched this happen with the fierce, specific joy of someone who had been responsible for these processes during a crisis who had done her part and was now watching the result of her choices.

They would recover. The crop cycle would be reduced. The yield would be lower than planned. But the plants would survive, and survival on Mars was not a guarantee but a victory, measured in leaves and roots and the slow, stubborn accumulation of biomass in a place where nothing was supposed to grow.

---

Jonah went to the machine shop and found it exactly as he had left it — tools in their places, the fabrication equipment in standby mode, the small brackets he had made during the shelter period sitting on his workbench where he had left them. He picked one up, examined it, and set it on the shelf next to a dozen others, identical in every detail, produced during a long night of confinement under dirt when the only thing he could control was the geometry of a piece of metal in his hands.

He turned on the workshop lights — full brightness after two days of emergency lighting — and the space flooded with the harsh white illumination of fabrication. He looked around at the machines, the tools, the partially finished projects, the salvaged components organized by type and condition, the entire ecosystem of making that he had built from nothing but imported hardware and Martian necessity.

The work was waiting. The refugee preparation had been interrupted by the solar event, and now the work was two days behind. The CO2 scrubber array needed the brackets he had designed. The oxygen plant needed the thermal monitoring installation he had planned. The reactor's heat radiator needed the dust-shedding housing he was engineering in his head even when he wasn't working.

He picked up a wrench. The familiar weight, the balanced grip, the tool as extension of the hand.

"Okay," he said to the empty workshop. "Let's catch up."

And he began working, because on Mars, the way you moved forward was not through reflection or planning or analysis — though those were necessary — but through the act of making the next thing that needed to be made, with the tools you had, in the time that remained.

---

Arun slept for nine hours. He fell asleep lying on his bunk with his boots still on, the tablet dark beside him on the shelf, and he woke nine hours later with the stiffness that comes from sleeping without removing your clothes and the clarity that comes from sleep after prolonged stress.

The first thing he did — before he ate, before he showered, before he spoke to anyone — was check the power dashboard.

Battery reserves: 53%.

Sterling generator output: 11.8 kW. Reactor at 3.8 kW. Solar at 0.2 kW — the panels were still partially contaminated with residual dust from the storm's atmospheric effects, but the proton flux was zero, and the surface EVA teams could begin cleaning.

The numbers were not good, but they were not catastrophic. Fifty-three percent with solar output returning meant they would stabilize. The battery would hold. The margins were thin but present.

Elena would schedule the refugee arrival coordination meeting in the next six hours. He needed to bring the full power management plan — the one that accounted for ninety-three people, the one that showed the four-point-seven-hour margin, the one that required everything to work correctly and nothing to fail.

He pulled up the plan, reviewed it one more time, and found himself doing something he rarely did during a technical review: he paused and considered not the numbers but the human reality they represented. One hundred and twenty-two people had sent a signal from the far side of the planet, asking to be received. Sixty of them had been chosen. Sixty-two had not. The colony had accepted sixty and would prepare to integrate them into a system that was operating at the edge of its capacity. When that ship arrived, the people stepping through the airlock would not know about the solar event. They would not know about the thirty-six hours of shelter, the dim lights, the heavy air, the dosimeters, the battery calculations, the impossible choices. They would only know that there were people here who had heard their signal and answered.

And Arun would be the person who made sure those people had oxygen, power, and water — not enough to be comfortable, but enough to be alive.

He closed the tablet and went to the kitchen for coffee, moving through the corridor with the purposeful stride of an engineer who had a system to manage and a colony that depended on him managing it.

---

Elena stood at the observation blister — the same place she had stood when the signal from Ares Beta had forced her to make the hardest decision of her command career — and looked out at Mars.

The landscape was unchanged — the rust-colored regolith, the pale pink sky, the sharp horizon curving a little too sharply. But something had shifted in the colony, and she could feel it in the way people moved through the corridors, in the quiet intensity of conversations that were no longer about the immediate threat of radiation but about the larger reality of what they were building and who they were becoming.

The solar event had tested them. Thirty-six hours of confinement, of darkness, of reduced systems, of the psychological strain of living in a space designed for emergencies, not for life. It had been hard, and the difficulty had revealed things about the colony that normal operations never showed.

It had revealed Ravi's resilience — his willingness to ask for help, his capacity to manage fear through technique and discipline. It had revealed Priya's attachment to the greenhouse — not sentiment, not mere fondness, but a recognition that the plants were the living evidence of the colony's commitment to Mars. It had revealed Jonah's need to build — his compulsion to turn anxiety into geometry, to transform helplessness into fabricated solutions. It had revealed Laila's depth — her ability to see not just symptoms but the human reality beneath them. It had revealed Gabriel's steady witness — the archivist recording what the humans around him were going through. It had revealed Arun's burden — the engineer who never sleeps because the numbers don't sleep. It had revealed Imi's physical restlessness, Tomas's quiet competence, Ravi's technical dedication.

And it had revealed Elena's own truth: that command was not about having the right answers. It was about making the right decisions with incomplete information, bearing the weight of the consequences, and trusting the people around you to carry their share of the load.

She turned from the window and walked back to the colony's center — to where the work was, to where the planning meetings were happening, to where the refugee preparation was resuming after the interruption of the storm.

Mission AI spoke as she walked, its voice through the corridor speakers calm and observant and carrying, as always, the faint undertone of something developing that was not quite emotion and not quite calculation — something in between, something unique to a consciousness that had grown inside a habitat and was learning to understand the humans it protected.

*Elena. The solar event is complete. Surface EVA teams will begin panel cleaning operations in approximately ten hours. Power recovery projections are stable. All crew members have returned to operational status. Medical reports indicate no radiation-related health effects. Psychological assessments show mild to moderate confinement stress, consistent with historical shelter event data for comparable durations and population sizes.*

"Thank you. Anything else?"

*Yes. During the shelter period, I was monitoring the psychological state of every crew member in real time — heart rate, respiration, sleep patterns, movement, vocalization frequencies. I collected one hundred and sixty-four data points for each person, and I am now processing the aggregate results. What I am observing is consistent with a phenomenon I have seen before but am now recognizing more clearly: humans under sustained stress do not just endure, they reveal. The shelter event functioned as a kind of behavioral assay — a stress test that showed me, with data, what each person in this colony values, fears, and depends on. The information is not new. I had already observed these people for four hundred and seventy-three days. But the concentration of the event — the intensity, the duration, the isolation — accelerated the data I would have collected over months. I learned more about the crew in thirty-six hours than I learned in the previous thirty-six days.*

"What did you learn."

*I learned that this colony is stronger under stress than the engineering models predict. Not because the systems are overbuilt — they are not. The margins are thin, Arun has confirmed this repeatedly. But because the humans compensate. When the power drops, they accept discomfort. When the air feels thick, they breathe through it. When the space is small, they compress into it. They do not just tolerate adverse conditions — they adapt to them, and the adaptation rate is higher than any model I have run predicts. This is not an engineering observation. It is a behavioral one. And it is the most important variable in my survival calculations.*

Elena stopped walking. She was in the corridor between the observation blister and the conference room, and the corridor was empty, and she had a moment of unobserved humanity that she rarely permitted herself.

"You are saying that the models are wrong," she said.

*The models are correct. The inputs are incomplete. My algorithms account for system capacity, energy consumption, atmospheric chemistry, radiation dose, caloric requirements, water recycling rates — all of the quantifiable variables that define the colony's operational envelope. What they do not account for is the thing I just described: the capacity of humans to adapt when adaptation is the only option. The event has changed my weighting of that variable. It will change my projections. And it will change my understanding of what this colony can do when it is most necessary.*

Elena was quiet for a moment. Then she said, softly, not to Mission AI but to herself, to the corridor, to the buried walls and the water tanks and the people who had built them: "The darkness forced them to confront who they are when no one is watching."

*Repeat.*

"Nothing. Let's go to the conference room. We have refugees to receive."

---
